content.rationale: Lorenz shows the collapse happens with zero argumentative content in humans; Choi et al. 2025 examine persuasion in debate. Which channel dominates in LLMs determines whether retrieval-mediated staging should gate exposure volume (how many peer answers are seen) or exposure content (rationales vs bare answers) — these imply different designs and different predictions for D5.

incoming_links.rationale: The agreement-intensity result shows that prompting agents to agree more raises accuracy on MedQA/PubMedQA but lowers it on counter-intuitive CIAR, and that a forced-disagreeing devil agent degrades performance even when the first answer is correct — evidence that the effect of peer exposure on accuracy is moderated by task truth-topology, relevant to whether diversity collapse arises from mere answer exposure.
Bounds rq1 from the rationale side: Choi shows conformity under full-argument exposure and provides no bare-answer condition, so answer-only sufficiency remains experimentally open.

content.acceptance_condition: A study with ground-truth tasks, mixed-capability LLM agents at varied majority/minority and capability configurations, measuring both answer-shift rates (conformity) and group accuracy pre/post exposure, under matched total inference compute.
content.rationale: Choi's topics are deliberately ground-truth-free, so its conformity rates measure persuasion, not accuracy. The note's mechanism needs to know whether the capability-dominance effect (one strong agent outweighs a majority) is error-correcting (strong agent is right and pulls the group toward truth) or error-amplifying (strong agent is confidently wrong and collapses diversity) on verifiable tasks - this determines whether staged retrieval should amplify or dampen high-capability voices.
content.text: Do Choi-style conformity dynamics - majority pull dominated by single high-capability agents, and minority capitulation - reproduce on tasks with verifiable ground truth, and when they occur, do they reduce or increase aggregate error relative to independent sampling?

To strengthen this claim, we demonstrated that a simple
prompt-based manipulation of the degree to which agents

could provide significant performance gains. By tuning this
